name: Treaty with the Shawnee, 1831 (Treaty of Wapakoneta)
nations: Shawnee of Wapakoneta and Hog Creek, Ohio, today the Shawnee Tribe and the Absentee Shawnee Tribe
promises: The United States would remove the band west of the Mississippi and grant it by patent in fee simple 100,000 acres within the tract granted to the Missouri Shawnee in 1825 (Article 2).
Removal costs and a year's provisions after arrival (Article 3), a sawmill, gristmill and blacksmith shop paid from the land sales (Article 4), and a $13,000 advance for improvements (Article 5).
The United States would expose the ceded Ohio lands to public sale to the highest bidder; after set deductions the balance would form a tribal fund paying the chiefs 5 percent a year (Article 7).
The granted lands would never be within any State or Territory or subject to its laws, and the President would protect the band there (Article 10).

breaches.what: The Supreme Court agreed with the Court of Claims that the United States failed to observe Article 7 and violated its trust by selling most of the ceded Ohio land at private sale for $1.25 an acre without first exposing it to public sale to the highest bidder; it held the Shawnee entitled to interest on the balance and remanded for recomputation at $1.25 an acre.
breaches.whoFoundIt: United States v. Blackfeather, 155 U.S. 180 (1894), on appeal from the Court of Claims (28 Ct. Cl. 447)

breaches.what: The Court of Claims found that the United States failed to perform its Article 2 stipulation to give the band 100,000 acres, and that it instead paid the Ohio Shawnees $66,246.23, taking receipts stating this was in full payment of claims under that part of the treaty.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Court of Claims, finding VII in the Shawnee case decided under the Act of October 1, 1890, as set out in United States v. Blackfeather, 155 U.S. 180, 184-185 (1894)

source.title: United States v. Blackfeather, 155 U.S. 180 (1894), statement of the case
source.publisher: U.S. Government Publishing Office, United States Reports

breaches.quote: the United States failed to perform their stipulation in this regard

landTaken: The two Ohio reservations granted in 1817, ten miles square at Wapakoneta and twenty-five square miles at Hog Creek (Article 1), Royce Areas 165 and 166; the Court of Claims found the cession totalled 96,051.48 acres.
compensation: The Court of Claims decreed $262,152.02 due to the Shawnees as of June 12, 1893, of which $260,999.24 rested on the 1831 account. The Supreme Court recomputed the 1831 lands at $1.25 an acre, giving $126,299.63 less the $87,257.63 already credited, or $39,042.00 due in 1840, with interest, and remanded. For the 100,000 acres the court noted that it did not appear the $66,246.23 paid was insufficient.
today: The final amount entered on remand and its payment were not traced. The 1825 Kansas tract within which the 100,000 acres were to lie was ceded by the Shawnee in the treaty of May 10, 1854.

nationVoice.summary: The Shawnee Tribe says that after the Indian Removal Act of 1830 the Shawnees of the Wapakoneta and Hog Creek reservations in Ohio signed a treaty that gave them lands on the Kansas reservation, and describes its people as pushed west by white encroachment.

nationVoice.nation: Absentee Shawnee Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma
nationVoice.summary: The Absentee Shawnee Tribe says that by 1832 the United States had removed the remaining Shawnees of the Ohio River Valley to Kansas.

openQuestions: The Court of Claims opinion (28 Ct. Cl. 447) was not opened; its findings are taken from the statement of the case in the Supreme Court report. The decree date of June 12, 1893 is the one the report gives; the Court of Claims decision date itself may differ.
Article 10's promise that the granted lands would never be within a State or Territory was not traced against later events; no finding on it was opened.
No account of this treaty by the Shawnee Tribe or the Absentee Shawnee Tribe was found in this pass.

plain.promised: 100,000 acres in the west, removal and a year's food, mills, and a fund from selling the band's Ohio land to the highest bidder, paying 5 percent a year.
plain.happened: The courts found the United States never gave the 100,000 acres, paying money instead, and that it broke its trust by selling the Ohio land privately. The Supreme Court ruled on this in 1894.
plain.today: The Supreme Court set $39,042 due in 1840, with interest, and sent the case back for recomputation. The final payment has not been traced.
